A12.title: Total ARG abundance (FPKM) and ARG gene richness by urban matrix and food-related contextual stratum in the curated ResFinder/KMA resource
A12.interpretation: Municipal wastewater (293 units, 7 studies, 63 countries) had the highest median total ARG abundance, 105,480 FPKM (IQR 67,379–189,060; bootstrap 95% CI of the median 96,717–115,653), and the highest median gene richness (89 genes). Medians in the other urban matrices ranged from 16,071 FPKM (built environment, 9 units) to 34,310 FPKM (transit surfaces, 24 units), with median richness of 53.5–60 genes. The food-related contextual stratum (155 units, 4 studies) had a median of 12,882 FPKM and 20 genes. Surface water was the most dispersed matrix (SD 0.83 log10 units; CI of the median 15,152–95,207), and median bacterial fragment counts ranged from 4,814 to 68,197. These are unadjusted descriptive summaries; air and transit surfaces each came from a single study, so their values cannot be separated from study effects (Table C08b).
A12.notes: FPKM, fragments per kilobase of ResFinder template per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments (relative measure); IQR, Q1–Q3; CI, bootstrap 95% interval of the median. Unit of analysis is the analytic unit (biological sample); descriptive only, no test.

A13.title: Mean abundance (FPKM) and any-hit prevalence of individual ResFinder genes, allele-collapsed for bla and mcr families, across all units and by matrix
A13.interpretation: The resource contained 651 ResFinder genes after allele collapsing of bla and mcr families. blaOXA had the highest mean abundance across all units (9,730 FPKM) and was detected in 78.8% of all units and 99.7% of municipal-wastewater units. The macrolide genes mph(E) and msr(E) followed (5,707 and 5,518 FPKM), then sul1 (5,269 FPKM), which was the most widespread gene (89.5% of all units). Means were sensitive to a few high-abundance units: blaKPC averaged 846.9 FPKM overall but was detected in only 6.9% of units, with a surface-water mean of 10,092 FPKM at 28.3% prevalence. Transit-surface units carried erm(X) and erm(C) at 100% prevalence. Prevalence reflects any-hit alignment, an upper bound, and gene detection does not indicate phenotypic resistance, expression or viable hosts; matrix columns are confounded with study.
A13.notes: FPKM, fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments; means include zeros. Prevalence, percentage of analytic units with any hit (551 units overall, including 155 food-related contextual units). MLS, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin. Descriptive; no test.

A14.title: Mean share (%) of total ResFinder ARG abundance by antibiotic-class group in each urban matrix and the food-related contextual stratum
A14.interpretation: Class composition differed markedly between matrices. In municipal wastewater, MLS genes contributed the largest mean share (37.2%), followed by aminoglycoside (17.7%), beta-lactam (16.1%) and tetracycline (14.3%) genes. MLS genes were even more dominant on transit surfaces (56.3%), whereas air units were dominated by tetracycline (40.9%) and aminoglycoside (35.3%) genes, with only 4.4% beta-lactam. Built-environment units had the largest beta-lactam share (30.4%), and food-related contextual units were led by aminoglycoside (32.1%), tetracycline (18.7%) and folate-pathway-antagonist (18.2%) genes. Fluoroquinolone/quinolone genes contributed at most 2.5% (surface water), and peptide/polymyxin genes at most 0.33%. Shares are compositional and descriptive; because air and transit surfaces each came from one study, these profiles may reflect study-specific protocols as much as matrix.
A14.notes: Values are unit-level percentages of total ResFinder FPKM averaged within each matrix; columns sum to about 100. MLS, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin. Food-related environment is a contextual stratum, not an urban matrix. Descriptive; no test.

C08.title: Linear mixed model of log10 total ARG abundance (FPKM) by urban matrix, with municipal wastewater as reference and a study random intercept
C08.interpretation: With a study random intercept, the municipal-wastewater reference had an estimated mean of 5.02 log10 FPKM. All other matrices had lower estimates: built environment −1.01 log10 units (fold change 0.10; 95% CI −1.85 to −0.17; p = 0.018), surface water −0.64 (fold change 0.23; −1.11 to −0.16; p = 0.008), air −0.88 (fold change 0.13; −1.90 to 0.15; p = 0.094) and transit surfaces −0.48 (fold change 0.33; −1.50 to 0.54; p = 0.36). The matrix term as a whole was supported (likelihood-ratio χ² 13.07, p = 0.011). Study variance (0.24) exceeded residual variance (0.13), giving a study intraclass correlation of 0.65. Air and transit surfaces were each represented by one study, so their contrasts are study contrasts; the remaining contrasts rest on two to five studies and remain study-limited.
C08.notes: FPKM, fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments. Fold change = 10^estimate. Model fitted to 396 urban units from 15 studies; likelihood-ratio test by maximum likelihood; ICC, intraclass correlation (study variance / total variance).

C08b.title: Study composition of each urban matrix in the ResFinder resource and the resulting identifiability of matrix effects from study effects
C08b.interpretation: The table shows why matrix contrasts were treated as study-limited. Air (24 units) and transit surfaces (24 units) were each sampled by a single study (100% of units), so matrix and study effects are not separable. The built environment comprised 9 units from 2 studies, one of which contributed 88.9% of units, giving only weak identifiability. Municipal wastewater (293 units, 7 studies) and surface water (46 units, 5 studies) were partly identifiable, with the largest study contributing 29.4% and 34.8% of units, respectively; the 2016 sewage pilot alone contributed 86 wastewater units. Only one study contributed to two matrices (3 wastewater and 2 surface-water units), which is too few for a within-study matrix contrast. Consequently, matrix differences in Tables C08, C09 and C15 cannot be attributed to matrix alone.
C08b.notes: Units are analytic units (biological samples). Largest study share is the percentage of a matrix's units contributed by its largest study. Identifiability is a design judgement, not a statistical test.

C09.title: Linear mixed model of ARG gene richness by urban matrix, adjusted for log10 bacterial fragments, with a study random intercept
C09.interpretation: After adjustment for sequencing depth and study, the matrix term was not supported overall (likelihood-ratio χ² 8.75, p = 0.068). Relative to municipal wastewater, only the built environment had clearly lower richness (−68.3 genes; 95% CI −118.7 to −18.0; p = 0.008), a contrast resting on two studies. Estimates for air (−29.7; p = 0.33), transit surfaces (−19.8; p = 0.52) and surface water (−8.0; p = 0.59) had intervals spanning zero. Richness was strongly depth-dependent, increasing by 49.9 genes per log10 unit of bacterial fragments (95% CI 43.0–56.9; p < 0.001). The study intraclass correlation was 0.58. The negative intercept corresponds to zero log10 fragments and is not interpretable. Unadjusted richness differences between matrices (Table A12) therefore largely reflect depth and study rather than matrix.
C09.notes: Gene richness, number of distinct ResFinder genes detected per unit. Model fitted to 396 urban units, 15 studies; likelihood-ratio test of the matrix term by maximum likelihood; ICC, study intraclass correlation.

C10.title: Linear mixed model contrasting food-related contextual environments with municipal wastewater in log10 total ARG abundance (FPKM), with a study random intercept
C10.interpretation: Food-related contextual units had lower total ARG abundance than municipal wastewater, by −0.62 log10 units (fold change 0.24; 95% CI −1.07 to −0.18; p = 0.006), with the stratum term supported by the likelihood-ratio test (χ² 6.79, p = 0.009). The estimated wastewater mean was 4.92 log10 FPKM. Study variance (0.11) was smaller than residual variance (0.22), giving a study intraclass correlation of 0.34, lower than in the urban matrix model. The contrast was not robust to normalizing by total trimmed fragments (fold change 0.40; Table SA03), indicating sensitivity to the denominator. Food-related units are processing and production environments from four studies and do not represent urban food systems; the result does not indicate food contamination, exposure or food-safety risk.
C10.notes: FPKM, fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments; fold change = 10^estimate. Model fitted to 448 units (293 wastewater, 155 food-related) from 11 studies; likelihood-ratio test by maximum likelihood; ICC, study intraclass correlation.

C11.title: Study-level mean log10 total ARG abundance (FPKM) with 95% t-intervals for each study and matrix in the ResFinder resource
C11.interpretation: The 20 study-by-matrix rows show that variation between studies within a matrix was comparable to variation between matrices. Municipal-wastewater study means ranged from 4.62 to 5.33 log10 FPKM, the highest being the 2016 sewage pilot (86 units). Surface-water study means spanned 3.86 to 5.30, and food-related study means 3.78 to 4.80. Built environment comprised one study of 8 units (mean 4.46) and a single-unit study (3.35) without an interval. In the only study sampling two matrices, wastewater (3 units; 4.89) exceeded surface water (2 units; 3.95), but the surface-water interval (0.75–7.15) was uninformative. Intervals for small studies were wide, and study means combine matrix, protocol, KMA version and depth, so they should not be read as matrix-specific values.
C11.notes: Values are means of log10 total FPKM per study and matrix; std, standard deviation; count, analytic units; se, standard error; 95% t-intervals. Descriptive; feeds Table C12.

C12.title: Random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) pooled mean log10 total ARG abundance and between-study heterogeneity for matrices with at least four contributing studies
C12.interpretation: Between-study heterogeneity was extreme in every matrix that could be pooled. Municipal wastewater (k = 7) had a pooled mean of 4.93 log10 FPKM (95% CI 4.74–5.12; τ² 0.055; I² 0.97; Q 216.0, p < 0.001). Surface water (k = 5) had a lower pooled mean of 4.45 (3.73–5.16) but much larger between-study variance (τ² 0.64; I² 0.97), and food-related contextual units (k = 4) had a pooled mean of 4.25 (3.79–4.71; τ² 0.21; I² 0.98). The surface-water interval included the wastewater pooled mean. With I² of 0.97–0.98, nearly all observed variation among study means reflected true between-study differences rather than sampling error, supporting the treatment of matrix contrasts as study-limited. Estimates of τ² from four to seven studies are imprecise.
C12.notes: k, number of studies with at least two units; τ², between-study variance; Q, Cochran's heterogeneity statistic (df = k − 1); I², proportion of total variation due to heterogeneity (0–1 scale). Units are log10 FPKM.

C13.title: PERMANOVA of ResFinder gene composition (Bray-Curtis, relative FPKM) by matrix with study-block permutation, study-within-matrix test and dispersion test (PERMDISP)
C13.interpretation: Among 396 urban units, matrix explained a partial R² of 0.21 of Bray-Curtis variation in gene composition (pseudo-F 26.27; p = 0.036 under permutation of whole study blocks). Study nested within matrix explained a similar share (R² 0.22; p = 0.001). When food-related contextual units were added (551 units), the matrix-or-stratum term had R² 0.23 but was not supported under block permutation (p = 0.068). Multivariate dispersion differed between matrices (PERMDISP F 28.97, p = 0.001), so part of the apparent location difference may reflect unequal within-matrix spread. With few studies per matrix, block permutation offers limited resolution, and the comparable R² values for matrix and study indicate that compositional differences cannot be assigned to matrix independently of study.
C13.notes: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity on relative gene FPKM. R², partial proportion of variation explained. Permutations restricted to study blocks (matrix term) or within matrix (study term). PERMDISP, test of homogeneity of multivariate dispersion.

C14.title: Spearman correlations between bacterial genus diversity and ARG diversity or total ARG abundance, overall and within each matrix, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment
C14.interpretation: Across all 396 urban units, genus richness correlated positively with ARG gene richness (ρ = 0.30; q < 0.001), genus Shannon diversity correlated weakly with gene Shannon diversity (ρ = 0.11; q = 0.053), and genus Shannon correlated negatively with log10 total FPKM (ρ = −0.27; q < 0.001). The negative pooled association was not reproduced within matrices: it was null in municipal wastewater (ρ = −0.05; q = 0.51) and positive in air (ρ = 0.71; q < 0.001), suggesting that it arose from between-matrix and between-study differences. Richness-richness correlations were strong in municipal wastewater (0.58), food-related units (0.58) and transit surfaces (0.86), whereas no surface-water correlation was supported (q ≥ 0.27). Richness correlations partly reflect shared dependence on depth, and unit-level correlations ignore study clustering.
C14.notes: ρ, Spearman rank correlation with 95% CI; q, Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p (p_BH). Unit of analysis is the analytic unit; correlations do not account for study clustering. Air and transit surfaces are single-study matrices.

C15.title: Linear mixed model of ARG gene Shannon diversity on genus Shannon diversity, urban matrix and log10 bacterial fragments, with a study random intercept
C15.interpretation: Among urban units, ARG gene Shannon diversity increased by 0.22 per unit of genus Shannon diversity (95% CI 0.14–0.30; p < 0.001), after adjusting for matrix, sequencing depth and study. Depth was independently associated with ARG diversity (0.36 per log10 unit of bacterial fragments; 95% CI 0.23–0.49; p < 0.001). No matrix contrast relative to municipal wastewater was supported: the built environment was closest (−0.68; 95% CI −1.37 to 0.004; p = 0.051), and the air, surface-water and transit estimates were near zero (p = 0.57–0.87). The positive within-model association contrasts with the weak pooled correlation in Table C14 and is consistent with community diversity and resistome diversity co-varying within studies; it is an association and does not indicate that bacterial diversity determines ARG diversity.
C15.notes: Gene Shannon diversity computed from ResFinder fragment counts; genus Shannon from SILVA rRNA alignments. Model fitted to 396 urban units, 15 studies; Wald p-values; variance components not reported in this table.

P08.title: Proportion of variation explained by the first ten PCoA axes and two-dimensional NMDS stress for Bray-Curtis ResFinder gene composition
P08.interpretation: The first two principal coordinates explained 18.3% and 10.4% of Bray-Curtis variation in gene composition, and the third explained 5.8%; later axes each explained 4.8% or less, declining to 2.2% for the tenth axis. Variation was therefore spread across many dimensions, and two-dimensional plots capture only a modest fraction of compositional structure. The two-dimensional NMDS solution had a normalized stress of 0.217, above the conventional 0.2 threshold for an acceptable representation, so distances in NMDS plots should be interpreted cautiously. No negative eigenvalues were produced, so no correction of the PCoA was required. Separation of matrices in these ordinations is visual and is confounded with study (Table C13).
P08.notes: PCoA, principal coordinates analysis; NMDS, non-metric multidimensional scaling (normalised Stress-1). Bray-Curtis dissimilarity on relative ResFinder gene FPKM. Proportions are percentages of total inertia.

T11.title: Bacterial genus-level diversity (SILVA rRNA alignments) and sequencing depth by urban matrix and food-related contextual stratum in the ResFinder resource
T11.interpretation: Median genus Shannon diversity was highest in air (4.88) and transit surfaces (4.88), intermediate in surface water (4.24), and similar in municipal wastewater (4.06), food-related units (4.06) and the built environment (3.95). Median genus richness followed a different order, from 1,454 genera in air and 1,191 in the built environment to 609 in municipal wastewater, 511 in food-related units and 411 in surface water. Median total fragments ranged from 2,499,100 in surface water to 40,846,000 in the built environment, and richness partly tracked this depth gradient. These are unadjusted descriptive summaries; air and transit surfaces each came from one study, and after adjustment for depth and study no matrix contrast in Shannon diversity was supported (Table T12).
T11.notes: Genus Shannon and richness from SILVA rRNA alignments (KMA); medians with Q1–Q3. Total fragments, median per unit. Unit of analysis is the analytic unit; descriptive, no test. Richness is depth-dependent.

T12.title: Linear mixed model of genus Shannon diversity by urban matrix, adjusted for log10 mapped fragments, with a study random intercept
T12.interpretation: After adjustment for sequencing depth and study, no urban matrix differed from municipal wastewater in genus Shannon diversity. Point estimates were higher for transit surfaces (+1.05; p = 0.14) and air (+0.96; p = 0.17) and lower for the built environment (−0.83; p = 0.17), with surface water close to the reference (+0.12; p = 0.73); all 95% CIs spanned zero. Depth had no detectable association with Shannon diversity (−0.025 per log10 fragment; p = 0.82). Study variance (0.43) exceeded residual variance (0.33), giving a study intraclass correlation of 0.56. Hence the apparent matrix differences in Table T11 are largely study differences. Because air and transit surfaces are single-study matrices, the model cannot distinguish their matrix effects from study effects.
T12.notes: Genus Shannon diversity from SILVA rRNA alignments. Model fitted to 396 urban units, 15 studies; reference matrix municipal wastewater; Wald p-values; ICC, study intraclass correlation. No likelihood-ratio test reported.

S04.title: Total ARG abundance (FPKM) and gene richness by continent in the 2016 Global Sewage Surveillance pilot (single protocol, mostly one unit per city)
S04.interpretation: Among the pilot units, median total ARG abundance was highest in South America (446,400 FPKM; 6 units) and Africa (419,900; 17 units), intermediate in Asia (253,900; 15 units) and North America (199,200; 14 units), and lowest in Europe (177,600; 31 units) and Oceania (172,000; 3 units). Interquartile ranges overlapped for several continents, for example North America (170,600–223,300) and Europe (136,700–231,400). Median gene richness varied less, from 130 genes (Oceania) to 162 genes (Africa). Because all units came from one study and protocol, these differences are not confounded with pipeline, but continents are coarse aggregates of heterogeneous cities, Oceania and South America were sparsely sampled, and the data represent one sampling round. FPKM is relative and does not measure exposure or health risk.
S04.notes: FPKM, fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments; Q1–Q3, interquartile range. Units are city sewage samples from one 2016 round. Descriptive; no test reported in this table.

S05.title: Mean resistance-class share (%) of total ARG abundance by continent in the 2016 Global Sewage Surveillance pilot
S05.interpretation: Class composition of sewage resistomes differed systematically between continents. MLS genes formed the largest mean share in North America (58.9%), Europe (51.4%), Oceania (47.1%) and South America (40.6%), but smaller shares in Asia (31.3%) and Africa (17.0%). African units instead had more even profiles, with aminoglycoside (22.9%), beta-lactam (19.2%), tetracycline (16.2%) and folate-pathway-antagonist (15.9%) genes; folate-pathway-antagonist shares were much lower in Europe (2.9%) and North America (3.0%). Oceania had the largest beta-lactam share (26.1%), based on 3 units. Fluoroquinolone/quinolone genes contributed at most 2.0% on any continent. Shares are compositional, so a lower MLS share necessarily raises other classes; continental averages also conceal between-city variation, and the profiles describe gene composition, not phenotypic resistance.
S05.notes: Values are unit-level percentages of total ResFinder FPKM averaged within continents; rows sum to about 100. MLS, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin. Unit counts per continent as in Table S04. Descriptive; no test.

S06.title: Global spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I) of resistome measures and Mantel distance decay among 86 city sewage units in the 2016 Global Sewage Surveillance pilot
S06.interpretation: All three resistome measures showed positive global spatial autocorrelation. With five-nearest-neighbour weights, Moran's I was 0.18 for log10 total ARG FPKM (z = 3.37; p = 0.0024), 0.21 for gene richness (p = 0.0009) and 0.14 for the beta-lactam share (p = 0.015), against an expectation of −0.012. Results were similar with eight neighbours for total abundance (0.14; p = 0.0033) and beta-lactam share (0.10; p = 0.018), but weaker for richness (0.088; p = 0.033). Resistome dissimilarity increased with great-circle distance (Mantel r = 0.20; p = 0.0003). These global statistics indicate that nearby cities tended to have more similar resistomes in 2016, but they do not locate hotspots, are based mostly on one sample per city from one round, and may reflect regional differences in sanitation or sampling.
S06.notes: Moran's I with row-standardised k-nearest-neighbour weights; two-sided permutation p-values (9,999 permutations); z relative to the permutation null. Mantel test, Spearman correlation of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity with great-circle distance. Unit: one sewage unit (mostly one per city).

S07.title: Feasibility of spatial analyses given the available data: requirements, data availability and decisions taken
S07.interpretation: Of the six spatial methods considered, three were performed (one restricted to the pilot), two were not performed and one was adapted. Observed-value point maps used producer-reported coordinates for 6,134 included samples, including 278 wastewater ARG units, and a country-level choropleth covered 106 countries. Global Moran's I and Mantel tests required comparable measurements at 30 or more locations from one protocol and were therefore limited to the 86-city 2016 pilot. Local hotspot statistics were not computed because sampling (one sample per city; sparse in Africa, South America and Oceania) would make hotspots artefacts of sampling gaps. Interpolated surfaces and risk maps were not produced because neither dense sampling nor outcome data defining risk existed. The 19 Indian open-drain sites lacked identifiers, so city was used as the mapping unit.
S07.notes: Design and feasibility table; no statistics. LISA, local indicators of spatial association; Getis-Ord Gi*, local hotspot statistic; IDW, inverse-distance weighting. Observed-value maps are not risk maps.

M01.title: Design of exploratory Model A, classifying municipal wastewater against other urban matrices from resistome class composition
M01.interpretation: Model A was a matrix-signature test, not a health or risk model. Its 396 urban units comprised 293 municipal-wastewater units (positive class) and 103 surface-water, air, built-environment and transit-surface units, drawn from 15 studies; the class imbalance means that a trivial classifier attains high accuracy. Features were the centred log-ratios of 12 class-group shares of total FPKM. Zero replacement (0.65 times the smallest non-zero share) and the log-ratio transform were estimated within each training fold, so test folds never informed pre-processing. The primary validation was stratified group four-fold cross-validation holding out whole studies, repeated 10 times, with leave-one-study-out runs for per-study accuracy. A study-ignorant four-fold scheme was run only to quantify leakage. With 15 studies, held-out folds contain few studies, which limits stability.
M01.notes: CLR, centred log-ratio transformation. Unit of analysis is the analytic unit (biological sample); grouping variable is study. Performance is in Table M02, per-study accuracy in Table M03 and feature importance in Table M04.

M02.title: Classification performance of Model A under study-grouped and study-ignorant cross-validation, compared with a prior-only baseline
M02.interpretation: With whole studies held out, the random forest achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.70 (SD 0.18; 2.5th–97.5th percentile of fold values 0.23–0.85) and a balanced accuracy of 0.59; gradient boosting reached 0.63, and logistic regression performed below chance (0.46). The prior-only baseline had a PR-AUC of 0.74, against 0.86 for the random forest. At the default threshold, the random forest's pooled accuracy (0.64) and Brier score (0.21) were worse than the baseline's (0.74 and 0.19). When studies were allowed to leak across folds, ROC-AUC rose to 0.93 (random forest), 0.91 (gradient boosting) and 0.72 (logistic regression). Most apparent discrimination therefore reflects study-specific signal, and the resistome class profile is a weak and unstable marker of municipal wastewater across studies.
M02.notes: ROC-AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; PR-AUC, area under the precision-recall curve; Brier, mean squared error of predicted probabilities. Metrics averaged over 40 folds (4 folds × 10 repeats); threshold metrics pooled from seed 0.

M03.title: Accuracy of Model A on each held-out study under leave-one-study-out validation, by model and study matrix
M03.interpretation: Accuracy on unseen studies depended strongly on matrix, indicating that both models tended to predict wastewater by default. For studies containing only municipal wastewater, accuracy was 0.80–0.95 for logistic regression and 0.62–0.87 for the random forest. For other matrices it was much lower: surface-water studies were classified with accuracy of 0–0.25 (logistic regression) and 0–0.375 (random forest), and logistic regression assigned mean wastewater probabilities up to 0.93 to surface-water units. Air (0.083 and 0.50) and transit surfaces (0.33 and 0.42) were also poorly recognized, whereas the 8-unit built-environment study was classified more accurately (0.75 and 0.875). The single mixed study (5 units; true-positive share 0.6) reached 0.60 with both models. Per-study accuracies for small studies, including a one-unit study, are highly unstable.
M03.notes: Each row is one held-out study (15 studies per model). True positive share, proportion of the study's units that are municipal wastewater; mean predicted prob, mean predicted probability of wastewater. Unit of analysis is the analytic unit within each study.

M04.title: Feature importance in Model A: held-out permutation importance and impurity importance (random forest) and standardized logistic coefficients
M04.interpretation: Feature importance was small and inconsistent across methods. In held-out permutation tests, only fosfomycin (mean accuracy drop 0.028) and multi-class (0.025) shares produced drops above 0.01, followed by fluoroquinolone/quinolone (0.0087); seven of the 12 class features had negative values, meaning that permuting them did not reduce held-out accuracy, the largest being phenicol (−0.017). Impurity importance from the full fit also ranked fosfomycin first (0.15), followed by tetracycline (0.11) and multi-class (0.10). Standardized logistic coefficients emphasized different features: Other (−0.90), beta-lactam (+0.58), MLS (+0.45) and fosfomycin (−0.32). Low-abundance classes therefore dominate the classifiers' signal. Because CLR features are mutually dependent and the models discriminated weakly across studies (Table M02), these importances are descriptive and do not identify matrix-specific resistance mechanisms.
M04.notes: CLR, centred log-ratio of class share. Mean accuracy drop, held-out permutation importance (random forest); impurity importance, mean decrease in impurity on the full fit; logistic coefficients standardized. MLS, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin.

M05.title: Performance of exploratory Model B predicting log10 total ARG abundance (RPKM) in Indian open-drain wastewater from CLR prokaryotic phylum composition
M05.interpretation: Under the temporal hold-out (training before September 2023, n = 332; testing thereafter, n = 115), ridge regression predicted later-month abundance with R² 0.52 ( 95% CI 0.28–0.67; MAE 0.110 log10 units; Spearman ρ 0.71), against a training-mean baseline R² of −0.023; the random forest reached R² 0.32 (0.13–0.53). Transfer to unseen cities was weaker and inconsistent. Pooled leave-one-city-out R² was 0.28 for ridge regression and 0.24 for the random forest, and held-out-city ridge R² ranged from −0.037 (Delhi) to 0.41 (Kolkata); random-forest values ranged from −0.53 (Delhi) to 0.63 (Kolkata). Rank correlations within held-out cities remained 0.63–0.68 for ridge, suggesting city-level offsets. Training and test samples share sites and one pipeline, so the model shows association, not a forecast of health outcomes.
M05.notes: RPKM, reads per kilobase per million sequenced reads; CLR, centred log-ratio of 21 phyla; MAE, mean absolute error; RMSE, root-mean-square error. R² 95% CI by bootstrap. Unit is the sample (447 samples, 19 sites, 4 cities); samples are repeated site measurements.

M06.title: Permutation importance of CLR phylum features in the Model B random forest on the temporal test set
M06.interpretation: Three phyla accounted for most of the random forest's predictive information on the temporal test set: permuting Proteobacteria reduced R² by 0.22 (SD 0.078), Firmicutes by 0.14 and Tenericutes by 0.13. Planctomycetota (0.046) and Lentisphaerae (0.030) contributed less, and the remaining phyla each reduced R² by 0.024 or less. Three phyla had small negative values, including Bacteroidota (−0.013), meaning that permuting them did not degrade predictions. These importances describe a random forest that performed less well than ridge regression (Table M05: R² 0.32 versus 0.52). Because CLR features are mutually dependent and importance reflects predictive association, the ranking does not identify ARG hosts or mechanisms, and taxonomy-based abundance prediction remains exploratory.
M06.notes: Permutation importance, mean decrease in test-set R² when a phylum's CLR value is permuted, with SD across permutations. Temporal test set: samples collected from September 2023 (n = 115). CLR, centred log-ratio; 21 phyla.

M07.title: Feasibility of predictive modelling targets given the available data: requirements, data availability and decisions taken
M07.interpretation: Of six candidate targets, two were modelled as exploratory analyses and four were not. Model A, classifying environmental matrix from resistome composition, was feasible because matrix labels and resistome profiles were available for 396 units from 15 studies. Model B, predicting normalized ARG abundance from taxonomy, used paired data from one pipeline (447 samples, 4 cities, 25 months). Disease or outbreak prediction was not feasible because no clinical or epidemiological outcomes were linked to samples. Clinical AMR prevalence was not modelled because surveillance indicators were not downloaded, country-level only and temporally mismatched with the 2016 pilot. Food-safety or food-business impact could not be modelled without food-chain or economic outcome data. Temporal forecasting was not attempted beyond the hold-out because series per site were too short and sites were unidentified.
M07.notes: Design and feasibility table; no statistics. GLASS, WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System. Performed models are reported in Tables M01–M06.
